content:
Sphaeridiinae is a subfamily of water scavenger beetles within the family Hydrophilidae. Here's what I know about them:

## Classification and Diversity
- One of the largest subfamilies in Hydrophilidae, containing around 50-60 genera
- Approximately 1,000 described species worldwide
- Key genera include *Sphaeridium*, *Cercyon*, *Coelostoma*, *Dactylosternum*, and *Agna*

## Physical Characteristics
- Generally small beetles, typically 1-7 mm in length
- Most species are oval to elongate-oval in shape
- Often black or dark brown in coloration, though some have reddish or yellowish markings
- Antennae with a distinctive 3-segmented club
- Maxillary palps usually longer than antennae (characteristic of Hydrophilidae)
- Many have punctate or striate elytra (wing covers)

## Habitat and Ecology
- Primarily terrestrial or semi-aquatic, unlike many other hydrophilids
- Commonly found in:
  - Dung (many are coprophagous)
  - Decaying plant matter and compost
  - Leaf litter
  - Margins of water bodies
  - Some species in truly aquatic habitats
- Adults and larvae are generally saprophagous (feeding on decaying organic matter)
- Important decomposers in many ecosystems

## Distribution
- Cosmopolitan distribution, found on all continents except Antarctica
- Highest diversity in tropical and subtropical regions
- Well-represented in temperate zones

## Life Cycle
- Complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult)
- Eggs often laid in moist organic matter
- Larvae typically have 3 instars
- Pupation usually occurs in soil or substrate

## Economic Importance
- Beneficial as decomposers
- Some species useful in forensic entomology
- Occasionally considered minor pests when abundant in agricultural settings

The subfamily has undergone various taxonomic revisions, and molecular phylogenetic studies continue to refine our understanding of relationships within the group.
